head.title: SQL Island: The Anti-Join Escape
head.teaser: After escaping SQL Island, your journey continues at the airport. Help a confused flight attendant uncover missing passengers, lost sunglasses, and unassigned seats by using powerful SQL anti-join techniques such as LEFT JOIN, NOT EXISTS, and NOT IN. Can you find what is missing before takeoff?
head.copyright: Emanuel Foster, Nathan Massicot, Jahnavi Patil, Nils Wildhaber, Leandra Willi. © CC BY 4.0

text-scene.text: After you escaped from the island you were stranded on last week. You decide that you want to visit the friends you made along the way while escaping and have a nice vacation on SQL island!

You arrive at the airport with all your luggage and get ready to board. At the gate the flight attendant tells you that they want to start boarding but the terminal gives error message, passenger count incomplete.

select-scene.text: It is the first day of work for the flight attendant, and they ask you to help them learn how to use the terminal system. To begin with, the first thing we want to do is check which passengers are currently registered for the flight.

text-scene.text:
After a few seconds, the complete list of passengers registered for the flight becomes visible on the screen. You have selected all of the registered passengers and you helped the flight attendant.
You just interacted with the terminal of the airport and found the correct solution. Every great SQL adventurer begins with a single SELECT. Keep that momentum going!

select-scene.text: Now that the passenger list is available, the next task is to verify which passengers have already completed the check-in process for the flight. You will need to help the flight attendant with this tasks too. The result should show the passenger id and passenger name from the checked-in passengers.
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT p.passenger_id, p.name FROM passengers p JOIN check_ins c ON p.passenger_id = c.passenger_id;

text-scene.text: Good progress so far. The passengers who have already checked in have now been successfully identified, but the resulting list is shorter than expected. It appears that at least one passenger is still missing from the check-in records.
You just connected two tables using a JOIN, one of the core operations in relational SQL. You’re starting to see how data can be combined across tables.

select-scene.text: However, the task is not finished yet. We have already identified the passengers who successfully checked in, but now we need to determine which passengers have not completed the check-in process and are still missing from the checked-in list so that we can finally start embarking on our holiday to the SQL island. (Use and LEFT JOIN with IS NULL)
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT p.passenger_id, p.name FROM passengers p LEFT JOIN check_ins c ON p.passenger_id = c.passenger_id WHERE c.passenger_id IS NULL;

text-scene.text: The terminal highlights the names that were missing from the check-in list. With that information, you can now clearly see which passengers have not shown up or completed the check-in process yet. Oh no, one passenger is missing! We cannot take of without this passenger. We need to find them to finally be able to go.
The flight attendant explains that a significant number of passengers usually arrive at the airport by bus, so it would be a good idea to also check the nearby bus station for any missing travelers.

When you arrive at the bus station, you notice a large group of people waiting for the next bus to the airport. At first glance, it’s just a crowded and ordinary scene, and there is no obvious way to tell who among them might be the missing passenger from your list.

Since you don’t have any direct identification, you need a more systematic approach. One possible method is to compare the list of passengers who have not yet checked in with the people currently waiting at the bus station.

select-scene.text: By cross-referencing these two groups, and potentially taking into account where each person is located within the station, you might be able to determine whether the missing passenger is among the crowd. Maybe you can find out who the missing person is by comparing the waiting persons with the passengers and check their location at the bus station.
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT p.passenger_id, p.name, b.location FROM passengers p JOIN bus_station b ON p.name = b.name;

text-scene.text: Nice work, you’ve successfully found the missing passenger. He’s standing under the street light just outside the main entrance, confirming his location from the bus station data.

After speaking with him, you learn that he and several others have decided to take the bus instead of boarding the flight to the island vacation. This explains why they never appeared in the final check-in list.

manipulate-scene.text: Now the next step is to update your dataset accordingly: you should remove the passengers who is confirmed to be taking the bus from the flight roster. This ensures that the passenger list only includes passengers who are actually expected to board the flight.
manipulate-scene.sql-check: SELECT p.passenger_id, p.name, b.location FROM passengers p JOIN bus_station b ON p.name = b.name;

text-scene.text: The passenger list is now accurate. You get back to the airport and boarding can finally proceed.

Suddenly, you realize something important is missing. You lost your pilot sunglasses. Thinking back, you are fairly certain you must have left them at the gate earlier. When you return to the area, you notice several pairs of sunglasses scattered across a table, likely left behind by different travelers.

At first glance, it’s not immediately clear which pair belongs to whom, as there are multiple similar-looking items with no clear labels or identifiers. To solve this, you need to determine which sunglasses do not have an assigned owner.

select-scene.text: By checking which items in the collection are not linked to any known passenger or record, you can narrow down the possibilities. The pairs that do not match any recorded owner should be the ones that belong to you. (Use NOT EXISTS)
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT s.sunglasses FROM sunglasses s WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT * FROM passengers p WHERE p.passenger_id = s.passenger_id );

text-scene.text: You pick the sunglasses up. They fit perfectly. Nice, you are ready for the vacation!

You finally make it onto the plane, only to realize that your ticket is missing and you no longer know your assigned seat. Oh no, you have to find out which seats are free. But you prefer to sit at the window, because you want to enjoy the beautiful view of the island from the plane.

select-scene.text: You now need to identify an available seat that is located next to the window and has not already been assigned to any other passenger. (Use JOIN with NOT IN)
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT s.seat_number FROM seats s WHERE s.seat_number NOT IN ( SELECT c.seat_number FROM check_ins c ) AND s.position = 'window';

text-scene.text: You settle into the window seat and take a breath as the plane readies for departure. But all of a sudden someone of the ground crew boards the plane and asks you for you help, since you were such a help to the flight attendant.
During boarding the ground crew had noticed several bags still moving along the conveyor belt that don’t appear to match any of the passengers who have checked in for the flight.

select-scene.text: To resolve this, you need to compare the luggage records against the list of checked-in passengers. Any bag that does not have a corresponding passenger entry can be considered unclaimed or unmatched.

text-scene.text: By filtering out all luggage items that do have a valid owner, you are left with only those pieces that have no matching checked-in passenger, making it possible to identify the stray bags that still need attention.

Before takeoff, the captain performs a final check to ensure that every crew member has been properly assigned a responsibility. During this review, it becomes clear that not all crew members have a corresponding entry in the duty assignments table.
To identify them, you compare the full list of crew members against the assignment records. Any crew member who does not appear in the duty assignments table is effectively unassigned.

select-scene.text: These are the individuals currently standing by without a designated task, waiting for instructions. Since you already doing such a great job with querying, you need to help the pilot to find the crew members without an duty.
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT * FROM crew c WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM duty_assignments d WHERE d.crew_id = c.crew_id );

text-scene.text: The captain gives a confirming nod after reviewing the results. The crew members who were previously without assignments have now been clearly identified, and the situation is fully under control. You can finally return to your window seat in the plane.

select-scene.text: Just as you sit down, the caterer come to ask for your help. The caterer needs to offload excess food before departure. Find all meal options that not a single passenger has ordered, so they can be removed from the trolley and the plane is lighter.
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT m.* FROM meal_options m LEFT JOIN meal_orders o ON m.meal_id = o.meal_id WHERE o.meal_id IS NULL;

text-scene.text: The caterer rolls the trolley away — the unwanted meals are off the plane, and there’s more room for snacks. You made it! All of the obstacles to your vacations are out of your way. You relax in the seat and can finally look forward to your well deserved vacation.
The plane touches down on the island. Sun on your face, SQL on your mind. What started as a chaotic morning of missing passengers, unclaimed bags, and unassigned crew has come to an end.

You have successfully mastered anti-joins by navigating various challenges. By applying LEFT JOIN, NOT EXISTS, and NOT IN patterns, you were able to identify the missing pieces of the dataset, from passengers who hadn’t checked in to unassigned window seats and other challenges.
You now have a robust toolkit for finding gaps in data and ensuring completeness in any relational database. Use it wisely!
